newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. environment agency chief laments budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: U.N. environment agency chief laments budget cuts.

text.p: The head of the U.N. environment agency lamented on Monday budget cuts caused by the United States and other key donors failing to pay their dues while demanding reforms in the U.N. system.

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, executive director of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) -- the only U.N. body based in the developing world -- told the opening of its governing council that budget cuts were undermining its ability to manage the environment.

"The lesson from the 18th session (in 1995) was that a programme although approved, cannot be delivered if financial commitments are not realised," Dowdeswell, a Canadian, told ministers and representatives from 100 nations in Nairobi.
"Member states have reduced their overall contributions to UNEP, while at the same time imposing ever-increasing responsibilities on UNEP," she added.
The Governing Council meets every two years at UNEP's Nairobi headquarters and is normally used to approve a programme on managing natural resources and improving the environment.
But this year's forum is being sidetracked by talk of reforms and financial woes facing the agency because of the reluctance of some Western donors to pay their dues.
Dowdeswell said 18 of UNEP's 58 member countries, including three major donors, reduced contributions last year while only 37 percent of member states contributed to its Environment Fund.
Key donors such as Japan, United States, Britain, France and Italy are reluctant to pay, arguing UNEP has become less effective since the 1992 Earth Summit.
UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link more funding to reforms in the agency.
From a budget of $160 million during UNEP's 1991-92 programme, budget provision fell to $105 million in the last two years and even then only $62.5 million was disbursed by donors.
UNEP is preparing a budget of up to $80 million for the next two years but many experts doubt the powerful West will pay.
The United States has spearheaded calls for a cut in UNEP's budget as part of its attacks on U.N. agencies it considers inefficient or outdated.
Dowdeswell defended her efforts to reform the agency but said reforms must go hand in hand with a sound financial base.

"An examination of UNEP's role and focus, governance and the pursuit of an adequate financial base are absolutely central to UNEP's reform. One principal must be paramount: Whenever a decision is taken jointly to pursue global programmes, full financing must be guaranteed and secured," she said.

"It is imperative that this Governing Council revisits the financial system of UNEP and offers radically new views that go well beyond piece-meal adjustments and efficiency of the status-quo," she added.

Dowdeswell outlined reforms implemented by her administration as the strengthening of management, upgrading of capacities and expertise of staff and transformation of UNEP into a more efficient and streamlined organisation.
She said better management of technology led to increased efficiency and a number of functions were being integrated between UNEP and the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs.
She said professional positions paid for by the Environment Fund had declined 12 percent in the last quarter.
Use of consultants and corporate contracts declined 74 percent from 1995. Dowdeswell said she planned a 9.7 percent cut in management and administrative support costs in the 1996-97 year.
Critics charge UNEP with lack of focus and say it suffers from a demoralised staff, isolation from other U.N. agencies and the low quality of staff it can recruit to its Nairobi base.
New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has promised to reform the entire U.N. system and has made reform a constant theme since his election last December.
Washington vetoed his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, charging him with failure to press reform of the 185-nation organisation with sufficient vigour.
